content: The Peruvian pepper tree, scientifically known as Schinus molle, is also referred to by several other names, including the California pepper tree, molle, pepper tree, pepperina, Peruvian mastic tree, and Peruvian pepper tree. This plant can grow as either a tree or a shrub, reaching heights between 5 and 18 meters. It is native to the Peruvian Andes, with the name molle derived from the Quechua word molli, which refers to the tree. The upper branches of the tree characteristically droop, giving it a distinctive appearance. The leaves of the Peruvian pepper tree are pinnately compound, measuring between 10 and 30 centimeters in length. Each leaf is composed of 15 or more leaflets. The plant is dioecious, meaning that male and female flowers are borne on separate trees. These flowers are small, white, and produced in abundance in axillary clusters. The fruit of the tree is a small, spherical drupe that is pink to red in color, with a leathery texture. Each drupe measures approximately 5 to 8 millimeters in diameter and is carried in dense clusters containing hundreds of berries. The bark, leaves, and berries of the tree are all highly aromatic. The Peruvian pepper tree is cultivated as an ornamental plant in various regions, including parts of North America, southeastern Queensland in Australia, and Mediterranean coastal areas. It has naturalized in these regions and is considered an invasive species in many subtropical areas. The pink or red berries, while not true pepper (genus Piper), are marketed as pink peppercorns, similar to the berries of its close relative, the Brazilian pepper tree (Schinus terebinthifolius). These berries contain volatile terpenes, which can irritate the mucous membranes of sensitive individuals. Therefore, it is recommended to use the berries in moderation when employing them as a condiment. Historically, the Inca utilized the sweet outer layer of the ripe fruit to create beverages. The berries were carefully rubbed to separate the sweet outer part from the bitter inner components. The resulting mixture was strained and left to ferment for a few days, producing a refreshing and nutritious drink. Additionally, the berries were boiled down to make syrup or combined with maize to prepare a nourishing gruel.
